topic: Quantum error correction in NISQ devices
text:
IDEA:  
High qubit leakage rates (X) in current superconducting NISQ devices cause significant logical qubit fidelity degradation (Y) because leakage errors convert into bit-flip errors that violate surface code error correction assumptions (Z), which can be directly tested by a leakage-aware decoder incorporating leakage-to-bit-flip conditional decoding to quantify logical error improvements.

BACKGROUND:  
Quantum error correction in NISQ-era superconducting devices suffers from leakage errors that standard surface code decoders do not explicitly model, leading to uncorrectable logical errors and limiting scalable quantum computation. While leakage detection and erasure conversion have been explored, the precise causal role of leakage-to-bit-flip error conversion in logical error degradation remains unconfirmed due to confounding noise sources and decoder limitations.

APPROACH:  
We implement a leakage-aware minimum-weight perfect matching decoder that explicitly uses leakage detection flags from qubit readouts and models leakage-induced correlated bit-flip errors in the decoding graph, operationalizing mechanism Z by capturing how leakage converts into logical bit-flips that violate surface code assumptions. We further isolate leakage’s causal effect through controlled leakage injection informed by Lindblad noise models and comprehensive error tomography on ibmq_montreal, complemented by control experiments using leakage reduction units (LRUs) and erasure conversion protocols to suppress or convert leakage errors without causing bit-flips.

EXPERIMENT:  
We evaluate logical error rates on the primary IBM Quantum Experience ibmq_montreal dataset, synthetic Lindblad-based surface code simulations with calibrated leakage injection, and experimental Rydberg atom array data exhibiting erasure conversion without leakage-to-bit-flip pathways, comparing four baselines: (1) surface code baseline ignoring leakage, (2) standard Pauli error decoders, (3) decoders augmented only for erasure errors, and (4) variational error mitigation lacking leakage modeling. Confirmation requires >15% logical error rate increase when ignoring leakage-to-bit-flip conversion, falsification if ≤15%; ablation removes leakage-to-bit-flip modeling to test necessity of Z.

NOVELTY:  
This work uniquely isolates and rigorously quantifies the causal mechanism of leakage-to-bit-flip error conversion on logical error degradation via a novel leakage-aware decoder combined with targeted leakage injection and tomography, surpassing prior approaches that either ignore leakage, treat it as erasure, or lack controlled leakage isolation—thereby providing the first decisive experimental evidence that leakage conversions critically limit NISQ quantum error correction fidelity.

topic: Quantum error correction in NISQ devices
text:
IDEA:  
Modeling and adapting to intrinsic time-dependent decoherence variability in superconducting qubits via an adaptive minimum-weight perfect matching decoder reduces logical error rates in surface code QEC by >20% on IBM’s 27-qubit Falcon processor datasets, confirming that fluctuating T1 and T2 cause syndrome extraction mismatches and decoding inefficiencies.

BACKGROUND:  
Current quantum error correction (QEC) on NISQ superconducting devices typically assumes static or average noise parameters, neglecting significant temporal fluctuations in qubit decoherence (T1, T2). These fluctuations lead to mismatches between syndrome measurements and decoder noise models, increasing logical error rates and limiting fault-tolerance thresholds. A rigorous causal link between intrinsic decoherence variability and logical error degradation remains unestablished, hindering targeted decoder improvements.

APPROACH:  
We develop an adaptive MWPM decoder that dynamically adjusts edge weights each syndrome cycle using time-resolved T1 and T2 estimates extracted from IBM Quantum Experience 27-qubit Falcon processor calibration data, directly embodying mechanism Z (intrinsic decoherence variability causing syndrome extraction errors). This contrasts with baseline decoders using static average noise or only spatial noise inhomogeneity. Additionally, synthetic datasets with controlled temporal noise fluctuations and stabilized static-noise datasets enable precise mechanistic validation.

EXPERIMENT:  
We evaluate on three datasets: (1) IBM 27-qubit Falcon processor experimental runs with native decoherence variability; (2) synthetic simulations embedding controlled, time-correlated T1/T2 fluctuations matching realistic device statistics; (3) static-noise datasets with intentionally stabilized decoherence parameters. Baselines include the non-adaptive MWPM decoder ignoring temporal noise variability, a neural decoder trained on average noise, a decoder modeling spatial but not temporal noise inhomogeneity, and a post-selection error mitigation decoder. The primary metric is logical error rate reduction relative to non-adaptive MWPM; success is >20% reduction confirming Z. The falsification test ablates temporal noise information by shuffling or fixing temporal labels; failure to reduce logical errors then disproves Z.

NOVELTY:  
Unlike prior work that assumes static noise models or uses average noise calibration, this approach explicitly operationalizes temporal decoherence fluctuations in decoding, isolating their causal impact on logical errors. The combination of real device calibration data, controlled synthetic benchmarks, and rigorous falsification protocols uniquely enables causal inference on intrinsic decoherence variability’s role in QEC performance degradation.

topic: Quantum error correction in NISQ devices
text:
IDEA:  
Sparse qubit connectivity in NISQ superconducting devices induces additional SWAP gate overhead during syndrome extraction, which directly increases logical error rates by compounding gate errors and leakage not captured by standard decoders, causing >15% fidelity degradation compared to fully connected architectures.

BACKGROUND:  
Quantum error correction (QEC) is critical for reliable quantum computation, but NISQ devices suffer from physical limitations, including sparse qubit connectivity that necessitates SWAP gates to implement error-correcting codes like the rotated surface code. Leakage errors in Rydberg atom-based and superconducting qubits bypass standard syndrome detection, further degrading logical qubit fidelity. Existing studies inadequately isolate how connectivity-induced SWAP overhead causally elevates logical error rates, confounding architectural constraints with noise characteristics.

APPROACH:  
We operationalize mechanism Z—the causal chain from sparse connectivity to SWAP overhead to logical error degradation—by systematically varying qubit connectivity graphs on a single hardware platform or in high-fidelity noise-calibrated simulations, explicitly tracking SWAP gate errors in an extended surface code decoder. By correlating logical error rates with the number of inserted SWAPs during syndrome extraction and normalizing circuit depth, the method quantifies how SWAP-induced errors propagate beyond baseline noise, isolating connectivity’s effect.

EXPERIMENT:  
Using the IBM Quantum devices’ rotated surface code benchmarks as the primary dataset, supplemented by the Google Sycamore QEC dataset (2019) capturing leakage effects and a trapped-ion simulator dataset with fully connected qubits and matched noise parameters, we compare logical error rates across three conditions: native sparse connectivity, optimized low-SWAP mappings, and ideal fully connected topology. The primary metric is the logical error rate difference, with a >15% increase confirming the hypothesis and <5% difference falsifying it. The falsification experiment replaces SWAPs with error-free logical permutations via software circuit transformations; if logical error rates remain elevated without SWAPs, mechanism Z is rejected.

NOVELTY:  
This proposal goes beyond prior work by explicitly modeling SWAP gate errors within decoding, controlling qubit connectivity on the same platform or in matched simulations to isolate its causal impact, and implementing a clean falsification test via SWAP-free circuit transformations. Existing methods either ignore SWAP-induced errors, assume ideal connectivity, or fail to link incremental SWAP overhead directly to logical fidelity degradation, thus lacking mechanism Z and its rigorous operationalization.

topic: Quantum error correction in NISQ devices
text:
IDEA:  
Leakage-induced syndrome misidentification (Z) in Rydberg atom-based NISQ devices (X) causes a >10% increase in logical qubit error rates (Y) because leakage errors evade standard quantum error correction and propagate unmitigated, a causal pathway operationalized by a leakage-aware syndrome decoder that explicitly models leakage signatures in syndrome patterns.

BACKGROUND:  
Accurate quantum error correction (QEC) is critical for scalable quantum computing but remains challenging on near-term NISQ devices, especially those based on Rydberg atom arrays that suffer from high leakage error rates. Leakage errors differ from standard Pauli errors by corrupting syndrome measurements and propagating undetected, which can substantially degrade logical qubit fidelity if not properly addressed. Existing QEC decoders typically ignore leakage-induced syndrome misidentification, limiting their effectiveness.

APPROACH:  
We propose a leakage-aware Surface Code decoder that explicitly incorporates a formal leakage error model into its loss function, penalizing syndrome patterns inconsistent with Pauli errors and indicative of leakage-induced faults (mechanism Z). This decoder operationalizes Z by tracking leakage signatures via extended syndrome pattern analysis and thereby mitigates leakage-driven error propagation. Control decoders lacking this leakage-aware penalty and baseline decoders (standard MWPM, neural network decoders trained only on Pauli errors, and erasure conversion without syndrome modeling) serve as comparisons.

EXPERIMENT:  
We evaluate decoder performance on three datasets: (1) the IBM Quantum Experience Rydberg simulator with artificially injected leakage and minimized other noise, (2) a synthetic Surface Code dataset with analytically generated leakage faults only, and (3) a superconducting qubit dataset from IBM hardware with experimentally measured leakage distributions. The primary metric is the logical error rate, with hypothesis confirmation requiring a >10% increase over the fixed Surface Code QEC baseline without leakage mitigation, and falsification if the increase is <5%. An ablation removing the leakage penalty term tests if logical error rates revert to baseline, falsifying mechanism Z if no significant degradation occurs.

NOVELTY:  
Unlike prior work that treats leakage as erasure or ignores it, our method formally models leakage-induced syndrome misidentification and integrates this into decoder training, enabling direct operationalization and validation of the causal mechanism Z. This explicit linkage between leakage, syndrome misidentification, and logical errors, combined with multi-platform datasets and rigorous ablation controls, provides a more decisive, interpretable, and generalizable understanding of leakage’s impact on QEC performance in NISQ devices.

topic: Quantum error correction in NISQ devices
text:
To operationalize the causal mechanism that high spatial variability in qubit T1 coherence times leads to disproportionate error accumulation during error correction cycles, our experiment will implement an adaptive decoding scheme that explicitly weights syndrome data by each qubit’s real-time calibrated T1 values. This decoder will prioritize error syndromes associated with qubits exhibiting shorter coherence times, dynamically adjusting correction strength and timing per qubit. Concretely, the decoder loss function will incorporate a T1-weighted penalty term that increases the cost of miscorrecting errors on weak qubits, thus directly exploiting decoherence heterogeneity to test if uneven T1 drives logical error inflation. By comparing this T1-aware decoder against a uniform decoder (which ignores T1 variability), we probe whether accounting for spatial T1 variance reduces logical errors, thereby validating the causal mechanism.

Datasets include the primary IBM Quantum Experience 5-qubit calibration sequences for surface code circuits, providing real-world T1 variability and error syndromes. Two additional datasets are included: (1) the Rigetti Aspen-9 7-qubit device calibration data, offering a different hardware topology and coherence time distribution to test generality of T1-driven error effects; (2) simulated surface code error syndromes generated with controlled, synthetic spatial T1 variability profiles, enabling precise manipulation of T1 variance magnitude and distribution to isolate its causal role. These datasets allow direct evaluation of how coherence time heterogeneity impacts logical error accumulation in diverse physical and simulated settings.

Baselines consist of the primary Surface Code baseline without adaptive decoding (which treats all qubits equally), a uniform minimum-weight perfect matching (MWPM) decoder, a decoder adapted only to average device error rates but not spatial T1 variation, and a randomized weight decoder that applies stochastic adjustments unrelated to T1 values. None of these baselines exploit spatial T1 heterogeneity as a direct factor in decoding, leaving them unable to modulate correction strategies based on coherence variability. By comparing their logical error rates per cycle to the T1-weighted decoder, we isolate the impact of incorporating the causal mechanism in error correction performance.

Primary metric is logical error rate per cycle, with thresholds set to confirm the hypothesis if the T1-aware decoder reduces logical errors by >20% relative to the non-adaptive baseline, and falsify if improvement is within ±10%. Secondary metrics include syndrome misclassification rate (errors in syndrome interpretation weighted by qubit T1), and logical error rate variance across device runs, where a reduction in variance would indicate mitigation of uneven decoherence effects. The falsification experiment involves ablating the T1 weighting in the adaptive decoder while keeping all else constant; if logical error rates remain statistically identical or improve without leveraging T1 differences, this would refute the causal mechanism by demonstrating uneven T1 is not the driver of disproportionate error accumulation.

topic: Causal discovery from observational data
text:
IDEA:  
Explicitly modeling latent confounders as latent variables within a dual-graph nonlinear causal discovery framework improves causal graph precision by disentangling true causal edges from spurious correlations induced by unmeasured confounders in high-dimensional nonlinear time series.

BACKGROUND:  
Observational causal discovery methods, such as PCMCI, often assume no latent confounders and rely on conditional independence tests; however, unmeasured common causes in nonlinear time series induce spurious dependencies that violate these assumptions, causing significant drops in causal graph precision. This challenge is prominent in real-world datasets like the NASA GEOS-5 climate data and human neuroimaging, where latent confounders are pervasive and nonlinear. Current methods either fail to model latent confounders explicitly or rely on linear assumptions, limiting their ability to recover accurate causal structures.

APPROACH:  
We propose a novel causal discovery algorithm that operationalizes the causal mechanism Z—latent confounders inducing spurious nonlinear dependencies—via a dual-graph architecture: one graph encodes observed direct causal links, while a coupled latent graph models latent confounder effects as latent variables inducing nonlinear dependencies. A specialized contrastive loss penalizes inferred causal edges explainable by latent confounding patterns, enabling disentanglement of true causation from spurious correlation. This architecture directly embodies mechanism Z by explicitly parameterizing and controlling for latent confounders in the joint optimization.

EXPERIMENT:  
We evaluate on three datasets—the NASA GEOS-5 climate dataset (primary benchmark), the Human Connectome Project fMRI time series dataset (with known physiological and cognitive latent confounders), and a suite of synthetic nonlinear multivariate time series with ground-truth latent confounders. Baselines include PCMCI (no latent confounder modeling), Granger causality (no hidden confounders assumption), TCDF (deep learning without latent variables), and FCI (partial latent confounder modeling but linearity-limited). The primary metric is precision@k on causal graph recovery, with confirmation defined as baseline methods suffering >15% precision@k drop relative to latent-free synthetic controls while our method’s degradation remains <10%. Ablation studies removing latent variable modeling and/or contrastive loss test falsification by checking if precision@k degradation persists or disappears.

NOVELTY:  
Unlike existing methods, our approach explicitly represents latent confounders as latent variables within a nonlinear dual-graph framework optimized via a contrastive loss, enabling direct disentanglement of latent confounding effects rather than relying on conditional independence or linear assumptions. This advances causal discovery in high-dimensional nonlinear time series by operationalizing the latent confounder mechanism Z and demonstrating robustness on both synthetic and real-world complex datasets.

topic: Causal discovery from observational data
text:
IDEA:  
Explicit modeling and reduction of Markov equivalence class ambiguity via an intervention-aware regularizer improves causal discovery precision in high-dimensional nonlinear time series with latent confounders, demonstrating that intervention-driven disambiguation of causal directions (mechanism Z) mitigates hidden confounding-induced performance degradation.

BACKGROUND:  
Causal discovery from observational time series data suffers notable precision drops (>10%) under latent confounding, largely because existing conditional independence tests fail to distinguish direct from spurious dependencies when hidden confounders induce complex nonlinear interactions. This problem is exacerbated by the presence of large Markov equivalence classes, which obscure edge directionality and causal structure identifiability due to limited interventional coverage, leaving causal graphs ambiguous and imprecise.

APPROACH:  
We propose EquivClass-Aware Causal Discovery (EACD), which integrates nonlinear conditional independence testing with Bayesian posterior estimation of Markov equivalence classes and an intervention-aware directionality regularizer that penalizes ambiguous edge orientations only when interventional data is present. This architecture operationalizes mechanism Z by explicitly quantifying equivalence class size and using interventional signals to reduce causal ambiguity, thereby disentangling direct from spurious dependencies and improving edge orientation accuracy.

EXPERIMENT:  
We evaluate EACD on the DREAM4 multifactorial gene regulatory network challenge dataset (primary), the Earth System Grid Federation (ESGF) climate time series dataset, and a synthetic nonlinear time series benchmark with controlled latent confounders and varied interventional coverage. Baselines include CAnDOIT (key baseline), PCMCI, TCDF, and NOTEARS, none of which model or regularize equivalence class ambiguity or utilize intervention-driven disambiguation. The primary metric is False Discovery Rate (FDR), with confirmation if FDR increases by more than 0.10 absolute when interventions are removed, and falsification if the increase remains below 0.05. Secondary metrics include precision@k and equivalence class size distributions.

NOVELTY:  
Unlike prior methods, EACD explicitly models Markov equivalence classes under latent confounding and integrates a novel intervention-aware penalty that reduces directional ambiguity only when interventions exist, isolating the causal mechanism Z. Existing baselines lack this mechanism and therefore cannot attribute or mitigate precision drops caused by equivalence class ambiguity induced by hidden confounders and limited interventions. The design of separate ablations to disentangle equivalence class modeling from intervention regularization further enables a clean causal test of mechanism Z.

topic: Causal discovery from observational data
text:
IDEA:  
Modeling temporally lagged confounders via adaptive lag-aware conditional independence testing under nonstationarity improves causal graph edge precision by mitigating spurious edges caused by delayed dependencies that existing methods fail to capture.

BACKGROUND:  
Causal discovery in nonlinear, nonstationary time series data is hampered by temporally lagged confounders that induce spurious edges and reduce precision in inferred causal graphs. Existing nonlinear conditional independence tests, such as those used by PCMCI, lack mechanisms to detect these lagged confounders under nonstationarity, conflating delayed dependencies with direct causal links. This results in greater than 15% precision drops compared to stationary baselines, limiting reliable causal inference in complex dynamical systems like climate teleconnections.

APPROACH:  
We propose Lag-Explicit Nonstationary Causal Inference (LENC), a causal discovery method embedding a lag-aware conditional independence test that dynamically adapts kernel bandwidths to local stationarity windows, explicitly modeling temporally lagged confounders. LENC incorporates a loss function penalizing edges whose dependencies appear only after lagged conditioning, directly operationalizing the causal mechanism (Z) that failure to model lagged confounders under nonstationarity degrades precision. Factorial ablations isolate the impact of lag-adaptive kernel bandwidth and lag-penalizing loss terms, validating their necessity.

EXPERIMENT:  
We evaluate LENC and baselines—PCMCI, PCMCI+ (improved conditioning without explicit lag modeling), TCDF (attention-based deep learning without lag confounder modeling), and kernel Granger causality (stationarity-assuming lag-aware method)—on the Climate Teleconnection Dataset, the Nonstationary Synthetic Time Series Benchmark (with controlled lagged confounders and nonstationarity), and a Physiological Multivariate Time Series Dataset (ICU patient vitals). Primary metric is edge precision, with hypothesis confirmed if PCMCI’s precision drops >15% under nonstationarity versus stationary baselines while LENC maintains or improves precision within 5%. Secondary metrics include recall, F1 score, and lagged confounder detection accuracy. The falsification test removes LENC’s lag-adaptive kernel and lag-penalizing loss; failure to significantly degrade precision or detection accuracy falsifies mechanism Z.

NOVELTY:  
Unlike existing methods, LENC explicitly and dynamically adapts to lagged confounders under nonstationarity via kernel bandwidth modulation and lag-conditioned penalization, directly operationalizing and empirically testing mechanism Z. This factorial and multi-dataset design disentangles lagged confounders from nonstationarity, rigorously establishing their causal role in precision degradation—something prior nonlinear causal discovery approaches and deep learning frameworks do not address.

topic: Causal discovery from observational data
text:
IDEA:  
Explicitly modeling domain shifts in temporal noise autocorrelation and nonlinear causal dependencies via a noise autocorrelation embedding and nonlinear dependence regularizer improves causal discovery precision and F1-score under limited samples in high-dimensional nonlinear time series.

BACKGROUND:  
Causal discovery from observational high-dimensional nonlinear time series often suffers >10% precision drops because conditional independence tests lose power amid complex dependencies and limited data. This problem is exacerbated by unmodeled domain shifts—specifically, changes in temporal noise autocorrelation and nonlinear causal interactions—that reduce the generalization of deep learning causal discovery models trained on synthetic data when applied to real-world datasets such as financial time series and climate data.

APPROACH:  
We operationalize the causal mechanism Z—domain shifts in temporal noise autocorrelation and nonlinear dependencies—by integrating a dedicated noise autocorrelation embedding layer that jointly learns residual temporal noise dynamics, and a nonlinear dependence regularizer that penalizes oversimplified linear conditional independence approximations, into a deep causal discovery framework. This architecture explicitly encodes and regularizes for Z, allowing improved adaptation to domain shifts unseen during training.

EXPERIMENT:  
We evaluate performance using three datasets spanning a complexity gradient: the S&P 500 stock returns dataset (primary real-world financial time series), the Earth monthly climate dataset (high-dimensional nonlinear dynamical system with seasonal noise shifts), and a synthetic nonlinear autoregressive dataset with controlled noise autocorrelation variations. Baselines include TCDF (Temporal Causal Discovery Framework), PCMCI, Granger causality, and a nonlinear kernel causal discovery method—all lacking explicit noise autocorrelation modeling. The primary metric is F1-score with thresholds confirming Z if (a) Earth climate dataset precision drops >10% relative to PCMCI and (b) S&P 500 F1-score drops >25% relative to TCDF (p<0.05 bootstrap); falsification occurs if drops are <5% or <15% respectively. Ablation studies remove the noise autocorrelation embedding and nonlinear dependence regularizer to test necessity.

NOVELTY:  
Unlike prior work that either ignores domain shifts in noise structure or relies solely on conditional independence tests, this method explicitly models temporal noise autocorrelation and nonlinear dependencies as learnable components, enabling controlled synthetic interventions and domain adversarial training to causally identify and robustly mitigate domain shift Z’s impact. This provides the first rigorous causal test isolating noise autocorrelation and nonlinear effects as the mechanism degrading causal discovery precision under realistic sample and complexity constraints.

topic: Causal discovery from observational data
