topic: Zero-shot generalization in reinforcement learning
text:
IDEA:  
We propose to improve zero-shot generalization in reinforcement learning by explicitly suppressing over-reliance on high-frequency pixel-level features through learnable spatial low-pass filtering integrated into the representation learning pipeline.

BACKGROUND:  
Zero-shot generalization failure in RL arises because policy representations often overfit to task-irrelevant pixel-level high-frequency details, leading to poor transfer across visually distinct but dynamically similar environments. Existing methods with pixel-level augmentations or contrastive learning reduce overfitting indirectly but lack explicit mechanisms to filter out high-frequency noise, limiting their ability to learn robust, abstract state representations.

APPROACH:  
We develop a novel RL architecture embedding a learnable spatial low-pass filter preceding the encoder, paired with a reconstruction loss that penalizes retention of high-frequency information, thereby directly operationalizing the causal mechanism Z—that filtering out high-frequency visual noise reduces overfitting on irrelevant details. This low-pass filtering module is modular and configurable, enabling ablations and controlled frequency-specific interventions to isolate its effect on representation abstraction and transfer performance.

EXPERIMENT:  
We evaluate on three datasets: (1) DeepMind Control Suite Walker environment (primary), (2) DeepMind Control Suite Cheetah environment (shared dynamics, distinct visuals), and (3) CARLA autonomous driving simulator (complex dynamic scenes). Baselines include DrQ-v2 (key baseline with heavy pixel augmentations but no frequency filtering), RAD (random crops without frequency suppression), CURL (contrastive learning relying on pixel features), and our own ablation without the low-pass filter but with reconstruction loss. Primary metric is zero-shot policy success rate on held-out visual variants, with >15% performance drop relative to our method confirming the hypothesis and <15% drop falsifying it. Secondary metrics include mutual information between encoded features and input pixels, and average normalized transfer success across datasets.

NOVELTY:  
Unlike prior methods that rely on implicit pixel-space augmentations or contrastive objectives, our method explicitly encodes the causal mechanism Z by learning to suppress high-frequency task-irrelevant features via a dedicated low-pass filter and frequency-aware reconstruction penalty. This allows targeted, frequency-specific interventions and rigorous causal attribution unattainable by existing baselines.

topic: Zero-shot generalization in reinforcement learning
text:
IDEA:  
Incorporating a learned, value-aligned contrastive state embedding within offline reinforcement learning enhances zero-shot generalization by explicitly encoding task-relevant semantic similarity that improves value propagation to unseen states.

BACKGROUND:  
Zero-shot generalization in reinforcement learning remains challenging because policies often overfit to task-specific data augmentations that fail to capture invariant features necessary across diverse environments. As a result, value estimations for unseen but semantically similar states are inaccurate, causing significant performance drops when transferring to new tasks or domains. Existing methods like PPO with augmentations or contrastive representation learning (e.g., CURL) do not explicitly encode task-relevant semantic similarity aligned with downstream value functions, limiting their generalization capabilities.

APPROACH:  
We propose integrating a dedicated contrastive embedding module into the Conservative Q-Learning (CQL) offline RL framework that learns a latent state representation by optimizing a similarity-preserving loss based on downstream value function similarity. This embedding captures semantic similarity beyond pixel-level features by pulling together states with similar value functions and pushing apart dissimilar ones. The learned embeddings replace raw states as inputs to the CQL value approximator, operationalizing mechanism Z by structurally enabling more accurate value propagation and estimation for unseen, semantically related states.

EXPERIMENT:  
We evaluate on three benchmarks emphasizing complementary generalization challenges:  
- D4RL MuJoCo dataset (primary) for offline continuous control generalization;  
- Procgen Benchmark for zero-shot generalization to procedurally generated, visually diverse environments;  
- Meta-World benchmark for robotic manipulation tasks varying in object properties and goal states.  
Baselines include CQL (no explicit similarity embedding), Behavior Cloning (BC, lacking value-based reasoning), Contrastive Unsupervised Representations for RL (CURL, contrastive learning not aligned with value similarity), and PPO with task-specific augmentations (no embedding-based value generalization).  
Primary metric is normalized cumulative reward for zero-shot generalization, confirming the hypothesis if our method improves over CQL by more than 15% and falsifying if improvement is under 5%. Secondary metrics include zero-shot policy success rate (>10% improvement on Procgen) and embedding clustering purity aligned with downstream optimal actions.  
Falsification entails ablating the similarity-preserving loss or replacing the learned embedding with random/reconstruction-based embeddings; if zero-shot performance remains statistically indistinguishable from the full model, mechanism Z is rejected.

NOVELTY:  
This work meaningfully differs from prior methods by explicitly aligning contrastive representation learning with downstream value function similarity, embedding semantic task-relevant structure directly into the value approximator. Unlike existing augmentation or contrastive baselines, which lack this alignment, our approach operationalizes a causal mechanism (Z) that enables improved value propagation to semantically related but unseen states, thereby substantially improving zero-shot generalization in offline RL.

topic: Zero-shot generalization in reinforcement learning
text:
IDEA:  
Introducing an adversarial visual distraction invariance loss in the encoder enforces abstraction from pixel-level nuisances, thereby improving zero-shot generalization in reinforcement learning by capturing task-invariant features beyond task-specific data augmentations.

BACKGROUND:  
Zero-shot generalization in reinforcement learning (RL) remains a key challenge because agents often overfit to visual distractions and pixel-level details present in training environments, causing significant performance drops when transferred to novel, visually altered tasks. Conventional methods like DrQ-v2 and CURL rely heavily on task-specific data augmentations or contrastive learning but fail to explicitly remove nuisance variables, resulting in at least a 10% decrease in zero-shot success rates on benchmarks like Procgen.

APPROACH:  
We operationalize the causal mechanism Z—insufficient invariance to visual distractions causing overfitting—by integrating an adversarial discriminator that classifies visual distraction types applied to inputs, while the encoder is trained to maximize the discriminator’s error. This adversarial loss forces the learned embeddings to discard distraction-specific information and retain only abstract, task-relevant features. The adversarial invariance loss is trained jointly with the standard RL objective, ensuring that policy learning depends on robust, invariant representations.

EXPERIMENT:  
We evaluate on three datasets: the primary Distracting Control Suite (with systematic visual distractions), Procgen Benchmark (procedurally generated diverse visuals), and DeepMind Lab (complex dynamic scenes). Baselines include CURL, DrQ-v2, RAD, and SAC+AE—all lacking explicit adversarial invariance enforcement. The primary metric is normalized cumulative reward on zero-shot OOD test environments; confirmation is defined as our method achieving less than a 30% relative drop in OOD reward compared to in-distribution, while baselines exceed this drop. Secondary metrics assess encoder mutual information with distraction labels (targeting near-zero) and zero-shot average episode return on Procgen and DeepMind Lab, expecting >10% improvement over baselines. We falsify mechanism Z by ablating the adversarial loss in favor of standard contrastive loss; no improvement or unchanged zero-shot performance disproves the hypothesis.

NOVELTY:  
Unlike prior methods relying on heuristic data augmentations or contrastive objectives, our approach explicitly enforces distraction invariance through adversarial training, providing a direct causal intervention that isolates and suppresses nuisance variables. This principled and modular enforcement of invariant representations enables cleaner causal attribution, stronger zero-shot generalization across multiple complex visual RL benchmarks, and rigorous empirical validation unattainable by existing baselines.

topic: Zero-shot generalization in reinforcement learning
text:
IDEA:  
Introduce a dynamic, task-conditioned hard negative mining strategy within contrastive reinforcement learning to explicitly increase negative diversity, thereby improving embedding invariance and boosting zero-shot generalization performance across robotic manipulation and continuous control tasks.

BACKGROUND:  
Zero-shot generalization in reinforcement learning often fails due to learned representations overfitting to low-level pixel details, which reduces abstraction and hinders transfer to novel environments. Existing contrastive methods like CURL rely on uniform negative sampling, limiting negative diversity and causing embeddings to inadequately capture task-specific intra-class variation, resulting in sharp drops (>10%) in zero-shot success rates under domain shifts.

APPROACH:  
We propose integrating a dynamic negative mining loss into CURL’s encoder and contrastive objective that adaptively selects diverse, semantically hard negative samples conditioned on task context, explicitly maximizing feature space separation between visually similar but task-distinct states. This component directly operationalizes mechanism Z by increasing negative diversity to enforce embedding invariance to irrelevant pixel-level changes while preserving sensitivity to task-relevant variations.

EXPERIMENT:  
Evaluate on Meta-World benchmark zero-shot manipulation tasks (primary), DeepMind Control Suite’s “Walker Walk” zero-shot domain shifts, and Procgen procedural generation environments, using zero-shot task success rate as the primary metric, confirming mechanism Z if success rate drops >5% under domain shift compared to in-distribution, and falsifying if the drop is <1%. Baselines include CURL (uniform negatives), DrQ (data augmentation without negative mining), SimSiam RL (no negatives), and SAC (non-contrastive), none of which implement task-conditioned negative mining.

NOVELTY:  
Unlike prior methods, our approach explicitly isolates and manipulates negative diversity via task-conditioned adaptive negative mining within contrastive RL, directly linking increased negative diversity to embedding invariance and zero-shot generalization through controlled causal interventions and rigorous ablations—falsifiable by removing negative mining and observing unchanged zero-shot performance—thereby providing a mechanistic and quantitatively validated explanation for zero-shot failure that existing baselines cannot replicate due to their lack of explicit negative diversity control.

topic: Foundation models for genomics and single-cell biology
text:
IDEA:  
Integrate an explicit continuous latent pseudotime variable within a variational autoencoder architecture to causally model single-cell lineage trajectories (Z), thereby improving gene expression prediction accuracy (Y) by capturing cell-type-specific regulatory dynamics (X) across diverse single-cell datasets.

BACKGROUND:  
Current foundation models for single-cell genomics, such as scVI and scBERT, lack explicit modeling of cell-type-specific regulatory elements linked to continuous temporal progression along differentiation trajectories. This omission leads to significant drops (>7%) in gene expression prediction accuracy, as they fail to capture context-dependent epigenomic variation critical for transcriptional regulation. Addressing this gap requires explicitly embedding continuous lineage progression information within single-cell representations to disentangle transitional states from mature cell types.

APPROACH:  
We propose extending a VAE backbone (similar to scVI) by incorporating a continuous latent variable constrained via a multitask loss to correlate strongly with pseudotime estimated from trajectory inference tools (e.g., Slingshot, Monocle3) on the Tabula Muris Senis dataset. This pseudotime-regularized latent space enforces temporal progression cues (mechanism Z) as a core component, jointly optimized with reconstruction and cell type classification losses. To isolate the causal effect of temporal modeling, we augment baselines (scVI, CVAE, scBERT) with pseudotime covariates or multitask objectives and conduct intervention experiments—including pseudotime randomization and ablations—to rigorously validate mechanism Z.

EXPERIMENT:  
We evaluate on three datasets with rich temporal dynamics: Tabula Muris Senis (primary), Human Cell Atlas (HCA), and Mouse Organogenesis Cell Atlas (MOCA). Baselines include scVI (without pseudotime), scBERT, PCA+random forest classifiers, and CVAE with discrete labels but no continuous pseudotime integration. The primary metric is cell type classification accuracy, with a confirmation threshold of >0.84 for the new model versus ≤0.81 for baselines; secondary metrics include gene expression Pearson correlation (>0.65 vs ≤0.61 baseline) and latent-pseudotime correlation (>0.7). The hypothesis is falsified if ablated or pseudotime-randomized models perform within 0.01 accuracy of the full model or baselines outperform the proposed method.

NOVELTY:  
This work explicitly operationalizes continuous pseudotime as a latent variable constrained by regression loss within a foundation model, distinguishing it from prior models that treat cell states as static or ignore temporal progression. By incorporating rigorous causal interventions, enhanced baselines with pseudotime covariates, and confounder disentanglement, it offers the first comprehensive causal validation that continuous temporal modeling drives performance gains in single-cell gene expression prediction.

topic: Foundation models for genomics and single-cell biology
text:
IDEA:  
Investigate how the quadratic complexity of full global attention (Z) in Transformer-based foundation models for genomics and single-cell biology inflates gradient noise and destabilizes training on long sequences (X), causing >10% drop in rare cell-type clustering purity (Y), by implementing a hybrid attention mechanism that dynamically switches to linearized sparse attention for sequences >1024 tokens.

BACKGROUND:  
Current foundation models for single-cell genomics, such as scBERT, struggle to faithfully represent rare cell-type-specific gene expression patterns, leading to substantial drops (>10%) in clustering purity measured by Adjusted Rand Index (ARI). We hypothesize this degradation stems from underrepresentation of rare cell types compounded by gradient noise and convergence instability caused by the quadratic memory and computation complexity of full global attention on long sequences (Z). Existing approaches do not explicitly link attention complexity to training instability or embedding degradation, limiting their ability to generalize to rare cell types.

APPROACH:  
We propose a hybrid Transformer architecture that dynamically switches from full global attention to a computationally efficient linear sparse attention variant (e.g., Performer or Linformer) when processing sequences longer than 1024 tokens, directly operationalizing mechanism Z by controlling attention complexity as a function of sequence length. By instrumenting gradient noise scale and training loss variance during optimization, we isolate and measure the causal impact of quadratic attention complexity on convergence stability and embedding quality, especially for rare cell types.

EXPERIMENT:  
We evaluate on three datasets: (1) 10x Genomics PBMC scATAC-seq (primary, with long chromatin accessibility sequences), (2) Human Cell Atlas (HCA) single-cell RNA-seq (rich cell-type diversity including rare types), and (3) Tabula Muris single-cell transcriptomics (varied tissues and sequence lengths). Baselines include: (1) Standard Transformer with local attention (key baseline avoiding quadratic complexity but lacking global context), (2) scBERT with full global attention (no complexity reduction), (3) Performer Transformer with static linear attention (cannot isolate dynamic effects), and (4) Transformer with random attention patterns (lacking structured attention or complexity control). The primary metric is training loss variance, with >30% statistically significant (p < 0.05) increase indicating instability due to quadratic complexity confirming Z; secondary metric is ARI difference >0.1 drop in rare vs. common cell types confirming X and Y. The falsification experiment replaces dynamic switching with fully linear attention on all sequences; if training loss variance and ARI differences remain unchanged, Z is disproven.

NOVELTY:  
Unlike prior work, this approach explicitly links quadratic attention complexity to gradient noise and convergence instability through a theoretically grounded, dynamically adaptive attention mechanism that isolates sequence-length-dependent effects. It includes rigorous causal inference controls and falsification tests, providing the first direct evidence tying attention complexity to rare cell-type embedding degradation and clustering performance, beyond correlations observed in existing foundation models.

topic: Foundation models for genomics and single-cell biology
text:
IDEA:  
Preventing over-smoothing of cell-cell embeddings across developmental lineages via lineage-aware regularization in a graph neural network improves rare cell-type representation, leading to >7% higher cell-type classification accuracy and >10% better trajectory concordance compared to state-of-the-art baselines.

BACKGROUND:  
Current foundation models for single-cell genomics and transcriptomics struggle to accurately classify rare cell types because their embeddings become over-smoothed, homogenizing features across distinct lineages and obscuring transcriptional heterogeneity. This results in a measurable drop (>7%) in classification accuracy on rare cellular states, limiting biological interpretability and downstream analyses such as trajectory inference.

APPROACH:  
We develop a modified graph neural network architecture that explicitly models and constrains over-smoothing by introducing a lineage-aware regularization loss, which adaptively penalizes embedding similarity between nodes predicted to belong to distinct developmental stages or rare cell types. This regularization controls message-passing depth and preserves lineage-distinguishing features while allowing meaningful aggregation within homogeneous populations, directly operationalizing mechanism Z (excessive feature aggregation causing loss of lineage information).

EXPERIMENT:  
We evaluate our method on three well-characterized single-cell datasets: the Velten et al. 2017 hematopoietic stem and progenitor cell (HSPC) dataset as the primary dataset, supplemented with the Human Cell Atlas (HCA) immune cell atlas and the Tabula Muris mouse single-cell atlas. Baselines include CellChat (key baseline), scBERT, Seurat v4 weighted nearest neighbor (WNN) method, and GraphSAGE, none of which incorporate lineage-aware smoothing control. Primary metrics are trajectory inference concordance accuracy with a >10% improvement threshold over CellChat and rare cell-type classification accuracy requiring >7% improvement over scBERT.

NOVELTY:  
Unlike existing methods, our approach explicitly quantifies and controls over-smoothing by adaptive lineage-aware regularization, supported by quantitative embedding homogenization metrics and synthetic controls that isolate smoothing effects. Baselines lack any mechanism to prevent embedding homogenization across lineage boundaries, so they cannot recover rare cell-type signals as effectively. We also perform falsification experiments by removing or randomizing the lineage-aware regularization; failure to degrade performance in these ablations would refute mechanism Z as causal, providing a decisive test of the hypothesis.

text:
To directly operationalize the causal mechanism that local sequence context embeddings fail to capture critical 3D chromatin interactions (Z), we propose a foundation model architecture that explicitly integrates 3D chromatin contact maps into the variant effect prediction process. Specifically, the model will combine a transformer-based sequence encoder with a graph neural network (GNN) module that embeds chromatin interaction graphs derived from Hi-C or Micro-C data, linking distal enhancer-promoter pairs. The model’s loss function will jointly optimize for variant effect prediction accuracy and structural consistency between sequence embeddings and 3D chromatin contacts via a contrastive loss that enforces higher similarity between embeddings of spatially proximal loci. This architectural coupling directly tests Z by embedding and leveraging 3D structural information rather than relying solely on linear sequence context.

The primary dataset will be the gnomAD constrained non-coding regulatory variants set to evaluate variant effect prediction precision as anchored in the hypothesis. Two additional datasets will be included: (1) the Human Cell Atlas immune cell subset scRNA-seq data to assess model performance on rare versus common cell types, linking 3D structure-informed embeddings to cell type classification accuracy; and (2) a publicly available high-resolution Micro-C dataset from human lymphoblastoid cells to provide the 3D chromatin contact maps essential for graph construction. The HCA dataset is critical to test the cell type classification accuracy drop hypothesized to arise from insufficient 3D context, while the Micro-C data provide the physical interaction evidence necessary to operationalize Z.

Baselines will include Enformer, as required, which uses only linear sequence context and attention mechanisms but no explicit 3D graph encoding; scBERT, which similarly lacks explicit 3D chromatin information; DeepSEA, a convolutional architecture that also ignores 3D contacts; and a novel 3D-agnostic transformer trained on the same data but without graph integration. Each baseline excludes explicit 3D chromatin embedding and therefore cannot exploit mechanism Z. Comparing our model against these baselines on Precision-Recall AUC for variant effect prediction will test whether integrating 3D chromatin structure yields a ≥5% improvement, confirming if Z causally underlies performance gains.

The primary success metric is Precision-Recall AUC on gnomAD variant effect prediction, with a threshold improvement of ≥5% over Enformer. Secondary metrics include cell type classification accuracy differences on the HCA immune dataset (specifically assessing rare cell types with an expected ≥7% gap), and embedding similarity scores correlating with physical 3D proximity from Micro-C data. To falsify the hypothesis, we will conduct an ablation removing the GNN chromatin graph module, retraining the model with sequence input only. If this ablation yields no significant drop in performance on variant effect prediction or rare cell type classification compared to the full model, the hypothesis that 3D chromatin embeddings are necessary would be disproven, forcing the abandonment of mechanism Z as the primary cause of the observed predictive deficits.
